title: Trump Slaps 12.5% Tariff on 60 Economies as Global Trade War Reignites
content: The White House replaced its expiring 10% blanket levy with a new 12.5% tariff covering roughly 60 of America's largest trading partners and 99.4% of US imports, with the duties taking effect at one minute past midnight on 24 July. Rooted in Section 301 forced-labour investigations and hitting China, Vietnam, Brazil and Australia alike, the move rekindled trade-war fears, pressured risk assets worldwide and stoked inflation worries just as central banks turned more hawkish.
summary: A new 12.5% US tariff on 60 economies covering 99.4% of imports took effect on 24 July, reigniting global trade tensions.
context:
• The order supersedes the 10% 'global tariff' regime that was due to lapse at midnight, ratcheting the headline rate higher rather than letting it expire.

• The duties stem from Section 301 probes launched in March into whether 60 economies adequately enforce bans on goods made with forced labour.

• The escalation lands amid an already jittery market backdrop of resurgent inflation, higher oil prices and rising bond yields.
happened:
• Washington confirmed a 12.5% rate on 60 of its top trade partners, spanning China, Vietnam, Brazil, Thailand, South Africa and Australia, effective 12:01am US Eastern on 24 July.

• The trade office said the order covers 99.4% of US imports, a near-universal reach that leaves few supply chains untouched.

• Asian equities bore the brunt, with the Shanghai Composite down 1.61% and Japan's Nikkei 225 off 2.73% on the day as exporters slid.
implications:
• Higher import costs feed directly into US consumer prices, complicating the Federal Reserve's fight against sticky inflation ahead of its 28–29 July meeting.

• Trading partners may retaliate, raising the risk of tit-for-tat measures that would weigh on global growth and corporate margins.

• Import-heavy sectors — retail, autos and industrials — face fresh cost pressure and supply-chain reshuffling.
importance:
• Tariffs on 99.4% of imports represent one of the broadest US trade actions in decades, with macro consequences for inflation and rates.

• The move injects a fresh, hard-to-hedge policy risk into an already fragile market narrative.

• It sharpens the stagflation debate: higher prices alongside a potential drag on trade-dependent growth.

title: Wall Street Ends Bruising Week as AI-Spending Fears Sink the Nasdaq
content: US stocks limped to the end of a rough week, with the Nasdaq Composite closing Friday down 0.64% at 24,975.82 as investors recoiled from ballooning AI capital-expenditure plans, even as the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.46% to 51,947.25 and the S&P 500 finished virtually flat at 7,411.98. A rotation out of megacap technology towards more defensive corners of the market gathered pace ahead of next week's Federal Reserve decision.
summary: The Nasdaq fell again on Friday on AI capex fears while the Dow advanced, capping a volatile week for US equities before the Fed meeting.
context:
• Megacap technology has powered the 2026 rally, leaving indices heavily exposed to any wobble in the AI-investment thesis.

• Blowout capital-spending guidance from Alphabet and a profit miss at Tesla reset expectations for how much cash Big Tech will pour into infrastructure.

• Investors are positioning cautiously into the Federal Reserve's 28–29 July meeting amid firmer inflation and higher oil prices.
happened:
• The Nasdaq slid 0.64% on Friday to 24,975.82, extending a week in which it dropped more than 2% on Thursday alone.

• The Dow rose 235.60 points, or 0.46%, to 51,947.25, while the S&P 500 edged up 0.05% to 7,411.98 as gains outside tech offset chip weakness.

• Money rotated towards cyclicals and defensives as traders trimmed exposure to the most capital-intensive AI names.
implications:
• Leadership broadening beyond a handful of tech giants could reshape index returns and factor performance in the second half.

• Further scrutiny of AI returns on investment is likely to keep the biggest spenders volatile through the reporting season.

• A hawkish Fed surprise next week would add another headwind to richly valued growth stocks.
importance:
• Index concentration means shifts among a few megacaps drive outsized moves in benchmark returns.

• The week tested the market's core assumption that AI spending will translate cleanly into profits.

• The tech-versus-cyclicals rotation is a key tell on how investors are positioning for tighter policy.

title: 10-Year Treasury Yield Hits 4.70%, Highest Since Early 2025, on Hike Bets
content: The US 10-year Treasury yield climbed to 4.70%, its highest since January 2025, as surging energy prices and resilient labour data pushed investors to price in a firmer Federal Reserve rather than the rate cuts anticipated earlier in the year. With the FOMC meeting on 28–29 July, futures now imply meaningful odds of a hike later in 2026, a sharp repricing that rippled across bonds, equities and the dollar.
summary: Benchmark 10-year Treasury yields rose to a roughly 18-month high of 4.70% as markets priced in a more hawkish Fed.
context:
• The bond market had spent early 2026 betting on rate cuts, but sticky inflation and firmer data have forced a hawkish rethink.

• A renewed spike in oil prices tied to Middle East tensions has revived headline-inflation risk.

• The Fed's 28–29 July meeting is expected to hold rates while keeping the option to tighten firmly on the table.
happened:
• The 10-year yield reached 4.70%, its highest level since January 2025, up from around 4.49% earlier in the month.

• Futures priced roughly a one-in-three chance of a hike at the July meeting and a majority chance of higher rates by the autumn.

• Rising yields pressured rate-sensitive equities and drew flows away from risk assets, including crypto.
implications:
• Higher yields lift borrowing costs across mortgages, corporate credit and government funding, tightening financial conditions.

• A sustained move above 4.7% would challenge equity valuations that assumed an easing cycle.

• Bond investors face further duration pain if the hawkish repricing continues into the meeting.
importance:
• Treasury yields are the anchor for global asset pricing, so the shift reverberates far beyond the bond market.

• The move marks a decisive break from the rate-cut narrative that dominated the first half of 2026.

• How the Fed frames the inflation-versus-growth trade-off next week is now pivotal for every asset class.

title: Yen Sinks to Four-Decade Low Near 164 as Rate Gap Widens
content: The Japanese yen slid to around 163.8 per dollar, its weakest level in roughly four decades, as widening interest-rate differentials and a broadly firm dollar overwhelmed expectations of faster Bank of Japan tightening and the threat of official intervention. The relentless slide keeps markets on alert for Tokyo to step in, while a cheaper yen flatters Japanese exporters even as it stokes imported inflation.
summary: The yen fell to a four-decade low near 163.8 per dollar as rate differentials and a firm dollar pressured the currency.
context:
• The yen has been the standout G10 loser, weakening more than 10% over the past year on Japan's still-low relative rates.

• A rising US yield backdrop has widened the dollar-yen rate gap, encouraging carry-trade flows out of the yen.

• Japanese officials have repeatedly warned against 'excessive' moves, keeping intervention risk elevated.
happened:
• USD/JPY rose to about 163.78 on 24 July, the yen's weakest reading in around 40 years.

• The move came despite market expectations of further BOJ rate rises and speculation about currency intervention.

• The euro, by contrast, held near $1.14, leaving the dollar broadly firm but not uniformly dominant.
implications:
• A weaker yen boosts the earnings of Japan's big exporters but raises the cost of energy and food imports.

• Persistent weakness increases the odds of BOJ tightening or direct intervention, either of which could jolt global carry trades.

• Sudden reversals in the yen have historically spilled into wider risk assets via unwinding leverage.
importance:
• The yen is a core funding currency, so its trajectory affects global liquidity and cross-asset positioning.

• A four-decade low is a milestone that raises the stakes for Japanese policymakers.

• Currency moves of this scale reshape competitiveness, trade balances and inflation across the region.

title: Oil Whipsaws as Red Sea Attacks and Peace Talks Pull Brent Below $98
content: Crude prices swung sharply as Houthi attacks on Saudi tankers and a suspension of Caspian Pipeline Consortium loadings collided with reports of fresh US-Iran peace talks, leaving Brent to fall roughly 4% on Friday to settle near $97 a barrel after flirting with $100 earlier in the week. The volatility underscored how tightly energy markets — and the inflation outlook — are now tethered to Middle East headlines.
summary: Brent slid about 4% to near $97 on Friday as US-Iran peace-talk reports offset supply threats from Red Sea tanker attacks.
context:
• Middle East tensions have injected a hefty geopolitical risk premium into crude in recent weeks.

• Houthi strikes on Saudi tankers and a halt to Caspian Pipeline Consortium loadings threatened a meaningful slice of regional supply.

• The oil spike had complicated the disinflation story just as data had begun to cool.
happened:
• Brent fell about 4% on Friday to settle near $97 a barrel after trading close to $100 earlier in the week.

• Attacks by Iran-backed Houthi forces on Saudi tankers and a CPC loading suspension disrupted regional flows, briefly lifting prices.

• Reports of US-Iran peace talks then drained some of the risk premium, sending crude lower into the weekend.
implications:
• A sustained crude spike would feed straight into headline inflation and stiffen central banks' resolve to stay tight.

• Any serious disruption to Gulf or Red Sea shipping risks a far larger supply shock than currently priced.

• Diplomacy remains the swing factor, leaving prices hostage to Middle East headlines.
importance:
• Oil is the main channel through which regional geopolitics transmits into global inflation and rate expectations.

• Renewed energy volatility directly complicates the Fed's policy calculus into the autumn.

• Crude swings ripple across equity sectors, credit spreads and emerging-market currencies.

title: Bitcoin Slips Toward $65,000 as Rising Yields Drain Crypto Flows
content: Bitcoin eased to around $65,000 and ether fell to roughly $1,877 as higher US Treasury yields and fresh tariff-driven inflation fears lured institutional money away from risk assets, with spot bitcoin ETFs bleeding about $225m of net outflows on Thursday. Traders are also watching Washington, where the Senate faces pressure to advance the CLARITY Act, a crypto market-structure bill.
summary: Bitcoin drifted to about $65,000 and ether to roughly $1,877 as rising yields and ETF outflows pressured digital assets.
context:
• Crypto has increasingly traded as a high-beta risk asset, sensitive to moves in real yields and liquidity.

• Higher oil prices and new tariffs have pushed inflation expectations and Treasury yields higher, sapping appetite for speculative assets.

• US regulatory clarity remains a swing factor, with the CLARITY Act market-structure bill stalled in the Senate.
happened:
• Bitcoin opened Friday around $65,048, about 1.6% lower on the day, while ether slid roughly 2.9% to near $1,877.

• Spot bitcoin ETFs recorded about $225m of net outflows on Thursday as institutions trimmed exposure.

• Prices steadied late in the week even as Brent's climb toward $100 kept macro pressure on risk assets.
implications:
• Continued yield strength could keep a lid on crypto as safer income alternatives look more attractive.

• Sustained ETF outflows would signal waning institutional conviction and add to downside pressure.

• Passage of the CLARITY Act could reset sentiment by clarifying US market structure and oversight.
importance:
• Crypto's tight correlation with macro liquidity makes it a useful barometer of risk appetite.

• ETF flows now materially influence spot prices, linking crypto to mainstream portfolio positioning.

• Regulatory progress in Washington could unlock or deter the next wave of institutional participation.

title: Gold Holds Near $4,050 as Middle East Ceasefire Hopes Trim Safe-Haven Bid
content: Gold traded around $4,050 an ounce, steadying after a mid-week bounce on safe-haven demand tied to Middle East tensions, then easing as reports of US-Iran peace talks drained some of the geopolitical premium. The metal remains far below its late-January record near $5,000, having spent the first half of 2026 grinding lower even as bouts of geopolitical stress spark periodic rallies.
summary: Gold hovered near $4,050 an ounce as Middle East ceasefire hopes pared the safe-haven premium that had lifted prices mid-week.
context:
• Gold set an all-time high near $5,000 in late January before retreating through the first half of 2026.

• Safe-haven demand has ebbed and flowed with the intensity of Middle East hostilities.

• Rising real yields have provided a headwind for the non-yielding metal.
happened:
• Gold traded around $4,052 an ounce on 24 July, little changed after a mid-week rise on safe-haven buying.

• Reports of US-Iran peace talks pared the geopolitical premium that had briefly supported prices.

• The metal remains well below its January record near $5,000 despite periodic flare-ups in demand.
implications:
• A durable Middle East de-escalation would remove a key pillar of support for bullion.

• Higher-for-longer rates keep the opportunity cost of holding gold elevated.

• Renewed geopolitical or inflation shocks could quickly revive the safe-haven bid.
importance:
• Gold is a barometer of geopolitical stress and real-rate expectations for global investors.

• Its resilience above $4,000 signals lingering caution despite the equity rally earlier in the year.

• Swings in bullion influence miners, central-bank reserve strategy and portfolio hedging.

title: Tesla Crashes 14.5% in Worst Earnings Reaction on Record Profit Miss
content: Tesla shares plunged about 14.5% to near $320 — one of their sharpest single-day falls in years — after second-quarter results paired record revenue of $28.2bn and 480,126 deliveries with a steep profit miss, as adjusted earnings of $0.33 a share undershot the roughly $0.50 consensus. Operating income slumped 57% to $398m on aggressive price cuts, weaker regulatory-credit income and heavy spending, dragging the Nasdaq lower.
summary: Tesla shares tumbled around 14.5% after record revenue and deliveries were overshadowed by a sharp miss on profitability.
context:
• Tesla has leaned on price cuts to defend volumes, squeezing margins across recent quarters.

• Investors have increasingly focused on profitability and free cash flow rather than headline delivery numbers.

• The stock had run up on robotaxi and AI optimism, leaving little room for disappointment.
happened:
• Revenue hit an all-time high of $28.2bn, up 26% year on year, with a record 480,126 vehicles delivered, well above expectations.

• Adjusted EPS of $0.33 missed consensus near $0.50, and operating income fell 57% to $398m.

• The shares dropped roughly 14.5% to about $320, marking one of Tesla's worst post-earnings sessions and weighing on the Nasdaq.
implications:
• Persistent margin pressure raises questions about how quickly Tesla can convert growth into profit.

• Reliance on one-off gains and credits to flatter earnings may draw sharper scrutiny from analysts.

• Heavy capital spending on AI and new projects could keep free cash flow under pressure.
importance:
• Tesla is a megacap bellwether whose swings move the broader growth and momentum trade.

• The reaction highlights how unforgiving the market has become on profitability, not just growth.

• As an AI-and-robotics story, Tesla's guidance colours sentiment across the wider tech complex.

title: Alphabet Sinks as Record $205bn Capex Plan Overshadows 82% Cloud Surge
content: Alphabet shares fell despite a strong quarter — revenue rose 24% to $119.8bn and Google Cloud jumped 82% to $24.8bn — after the company lifted full-year capital-expenditure guidance to as much as $205bn from $180-190bn, sending free cash flow to negative $5.9bn. The eye-watering AI infrastructure bill crystallised investor anxiety over how much Big Tech is spending to chase the AI opportunity.
summary: Alphabet stock slid as a raised $195-205bn capex plan and negative free cash flow overshadowed a 24% revenue jump and surging cloud growth.
context:
• Hyperscalers are racing to build AI compute, with capital budgets ballooning across the sector.

• Alphabet's cloud unit has become a key growth engine, but the infrastructure to support it is capital-hungry.

• Markets have grown wary of AI spending that outpaces near-term returns.
happened:
• Revenue rose 24% year on year to $119.8bn, with Google Cloud up 82% to $24.8bn and a backlog swelling to about $514bn.

• Alphabet raised 2026 capex guidance to $195-205bn from $180-190bn, having spent $44.9bn in the quarter alone.

• Free cash flow turned negative at -$5.9bn, and the shares fell as investors focused on spending over growth.
implications:
• Soaring capex across hyperscalers supports chip and data-centre demand but pressures their own margins and cash flow.

• Investors will scrutinise upcoming results from other megacaps for signs of similar spending escalation.

• The market's tolerance for 'spend now, profit later' AI bets is visibly narrowing.
importance:
• Alphabet's capex sets the tone for the entire AI-infrastructure supply chain, from chips to power.

• The reaction underscores a shift in investor focus from AI revenue promise to AI cost reality.

• As a market heavyweight, Alphabet's moves carry significant index-level weight.

title: European Shares Slide as ECB Holds but Leaves Door Open to a Hike
content: The pan-European STOXX 600 posted its steepest one-day drop in more than two weeks, falling around 1.2-1.3%, after the European Central Bank held rates steady but President Christine Lagarde struck a hawkish tone that markets read as flagging a possible September hike. Lacklustre earnings, elevated oil prices and rising yields compounded the sell-off across the region's equities.
summary: European stocks fell about 1.2-1.3% after the ECB held rates but signalled it could still hike in September.
context:
• The ECB has been balancing cooling growth against inflation that remains uncomfortably firm.

• A renewed rise in oil prices has revived European inflation risk, hardening the bank's tone.

• The STOXX 600 had hit record highs earlier in the month before Middle East tensions capped the rally.
happened:
• The ECB left interest rates unchanged, but Lagarde's comments were seen as leaving the door open to a September hike.

• The STOXX 600 fell roughly 1.2-1.3%, its biggest one-day drop in over two weeks.

• Weak corporate earnings, higher crude and rising bond yields added to the pressure on regional shares.
implications:
• A hawkish ECB pivot would lift European borrowing costs and weigh on rate-sensitive sectors.

• Persistent oil-driven inflation could force the bank to tighten even as growth softens.

• European equities may struggle to reclaim record highs while policy and geopolitical risks linger.
importance:
• The ECB's stance shapes the euro, European bond yields and the region's equity valuations.

• A shift from cuts towards potential hikes marks a notable change in the policy narrative.

• Europe's response to the oil shock is a key input for global inflation and rate expectations.
